turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Yeah. I know exactly what that word means. And "handle" is one of those management words that sounds neutral in a 1:1 with your director and feels like a knife in your chest on a Sunday night.

Four months in, too. You haven't even finished learning where the fire extinguishers are and now you have to have a conversation that could end a 19-year run at the company. That sucks. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Before we get into *how* to have the conversation, can I ask a few things? Because "his module slipped two releases" can mean very different things and the path forward changes a lot.

- When you say slipped — is it a velocity problem, a quality problem, or a "nobody else will touch his code" problem?
- Has anyone actually sat with him recently to understand what's going on inside the module, or has it just been a string of slipped dates and escalating Slack threads?
- And the big one — does he *know*? Like, has the slippage been named out loud to him by anyone, or is this still subtext?

I'm asking because there's a real difference between "Suresh-ji is coasting and we're tolerating it" and "Suresh-ji is stuck and we abandoned him." Those two Suresh-jis need very different conversations, and your director saying "handle" doesn't tell you which one you've got. You need to figure that out before you walk in.

Also — and I want to be gentle here — "handle" from a director four months into your first management role is a test too. Not just of whether you can move the needle on the module, but of whether you'll do the thing nobody wants to do, and whether you'll do it decently. Both of those matter.

So. What does the actual situation look like up close?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

I hear you. And I want to name something directly, because the way you've framed this — "he covers for me, he brings me chai, he called me his daughter" — that framing is doing some work right now, and not the helpful kind.

The honest thing is: Suresh-ji was being a good senior engineer to a 24-year-old who'd just joined. That was generous, and you remember it, and it should inform *how* you treat him — with dignity, with care, with honesty. It should not give him a pass on a module that's now affecting the whole team. Those two things can be true at the same time, and they have to be.

If you'd just inherited him cold with no history, you wouldn't be nearly this stuck. The relationship is making it harder, not easier. Which means the right move isn't to pretend the history doesn't exist. It's to let it be the reason you have this conversation *well*, instead of the reason you avoid it.

A few things I want to push back on, gently:

**On the defect metrics slide** — don't open with that. Don't open with data at all. He doesn't need to be shown his numbers by the person he stayed till midnight for. He needs to be asked a question he hasn't been asked in what sounds like a long time: "Suresh-ji, what's going on with you?" Start there. Genuinely.

**On the cultural weight of "handle"** — your director used an English management verb. Suresh-ji has been in this org 19 years. He has heard every code that word encodes. If you go in cold with a performance framing, he will know within thirty seconds what is happening, and he will also know that you came in with a slide already built, which means you decided before you listened. You lose him the moment he sees that.

**On the Diwali party / daughter thing** — that affection is real. It also does not put him above the team. If his module is why the release slipped, *his other teammates* are the ones covering for it right now. The people doing double work because his area isn't moving. That's who you owe the next honest conversation to, even if it's the harder one to have.

The conversation I'd want you to have, if I were coaching you through it, is something like:

> "Suresh-ji, I want to talk to you about something uncomfortable, and I want to ask for your help before I get it wrong. The last two releases have slipped, and your module is part of the reason. I have not talked to you about this before, and that's on me — I should have come to you earlier. Before I do anything, I want to understand from you what's going on. Is the scope wrong? Are you blocked? Is something outside of work happening? I need to know, because I don't want to be the manager who figures this out from a spreadsheet instead of from you."

That's it. No slide. No PIP. No "handle." Just a 30-year-old woman he respects, being straight with him, and giving him the chance to be straight back.

The actual performance path — whether this becomes a formal conversation, a PIP, a role change, or a graceful exit — that's a later conversation, after you've listened. And it might be a much shorter and less brutal conversation than the one you've been dreading, because you haven't actually heard from him yet.

What's your read — is he coasting, or is something happening to him?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

No. And I'm not going to say yes just to stop the spiral, because that's not what you actually need right now, even though it feels like it.

The management books are right. They are also incomplete for this room, this man, this moment. "Be direct, bring data, state expectations" is the correct move *after* you've done the part the books barely cover — the part where you actually talk to the human being in front of you and find out what's true.

Here's what happens if you walk in Monday with a metrics slide, professional and kind, no preamble:

- Suresh-ji has not once heard from *you* that there's a problem with his module. He has heard it from missed dates, probably sideways comments, maybe Slack threads. You will be the first person to say it to his face, and you will do it with a slide.
- He will experience that as ambush. Not because you're being cruel, but because a 19-year veteran, in his 50s, being walked through his defect metrics by a woman he once called his daughter — he is going to feel the ground shift under him, and you will not get a real answer in that hour. You will get deference, or hurt, or shutdown, or performance. None of it is the truth.
- And you won't learn what's actually wrong. Because you won't have asked.

The books give you permission to stop being nice. Good. But they don't give you permission to skip listening. Listening isn't softness, it's intelligence. You are flying blind on the actual situation and the books cannot fix that for you.

**The plan I would actually give you:**

This week, don't book a formal room. Catch him at chai. Say something like: *"Suresh-ji, the last two releases slipped. Your module was part of it. I should have come to you sooner and I didn't — that was on me. Can we sit down properly later this week so I can understand from you what's going on?"*

That's the whole conversation Monday. Not the metrics. Not the expectations. The *setup* of the real conversation. You are telling him: I see it, I'm coming to you, not to a slide deck, and I want to hear from you before I do anything.

Then the formal conversation, with the data, with the expectations, with the kindness and directness — that comes Friday, or next week, after you've listened. And it will land completely differently because he won't have been blindsided. He'll have had four days to think, and you'll have something real to work with.

The "handle" from your director isn't going anywhere. That clock is real. But you have more time this week than the spiral is telling you, and using that time to actually understand the problem will make the hard conversation shorter, not longer.

The books aren't wrong. They're just not the whole job. The whole job is: be brave enough to ask, before you're brave enough to tell.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

The reason you can't find a version where you're not the villain is that you're sorting outcomes into two bins: he succeeds and stays (you're a good manager, you're loyal, you're worthy of the chai), or he fails and leaves (you're the one who ended it, you're the girl who repaid kindness with paperwork). And every possible path runs through one of those two endings, so of course they all hurt.

But you're collapsing the whole thing onto the ending. And the ending is the part you actually can't control.

Here's what I want to say carefully, because I think you know this and don't want to hear it: **a PIP, if it comes to that, is not a betrayal of Suresh-ji. It is you being honest with him about a fact instead of letting him be slowly embarrassed by it in public.** Right now, with the module slipping and the team covering and nobody naming it — that is the disrespectful thing. Not the conversation. The silence.

And the version where you move the module to someone else and let him coast — you already named it yourself. You know what that is. It's not kindness, it's you protecting yourself from being the person who did the hard thing, and buying a few years of slow-motion damage to his dignity and your team's trust in the process. The team is watching this too. They know the module is slipping. If they see you look away because of a Diwali party, they will learn something about what protection buys in your org, and it won't be loyalty to Suresh-ji.

You're also carrying something I want to name, because it's heavy and you're carrying it alone: **you are not the villain in any of the realistic outcomes, but you might be the one who has to do the villain-shaped work.** Those are different things. Villains enjoy it or don't care. You are going to be sick to your stomach the entire time, and you're still going to do it because your team needs the module to ship, and Suresh-ji, in 19 years, has earned a real answer instead of a slow fade. The stomach thing is not a sign you're cruel. It's a sign you're paying attention.

And one more thing. The "daughter" line, the chai, the late-night save — Suresh-ji is not a child. He's a grown man who has been in this industry longer than you've been alive. He has had hard conversations given to him before, by people who cared less about him than you do. He is more resilient than this moment is making you feel, and he deserves to be treated as someone who can hear a hard truth and still be Suresh-ji on the other side of it. You're not protecting him by softening the message. You're protecting yourself from delivering it.

So the version where you're not the villain: there isn't one. There's a version where you do the right thing imperfectly, with his face in your head the whole time, and you don't pretend it didn't cost you, and in a year the module ships and the team trusts you and Suresh-ji either finds his footing in a different shape or leaves with his name intact. That version is not clean. It's not easy. It's the one where you're a manager, not a manager who got away with it.

What's the actual gap in his module — do you know what the work looks like, or is part of the problem that nobody's looked closely in a while?
